package.title: Why Does Bread Taste Better at 140°C? 🍞

Why does toast turn brown and taste better than bread? In a toaster, dry heat starts the Maillard reaction between sugars and amino acids, building hundreds of new flavor molecules and brown melanoidins.

package.pinned_comment: What's your perfect toast: pale gold, or nearly burned?
package.script: You just ate molecules, your bread never had. That's what toast is. So why does it taste so much better? Bread holds two key ingredients: sugars, and amino acids, the building blocks of protein. Normally, they mostly ignore each other. But in the toaster, dry heat drives water out of the surface. Then, at around a hundred and forty degrees Celsius, they start reacting. It's called the Maillard reaction, first described in nineteen twelve. It builds hundreds of new flavor molecules, nutty, roasty, toasty. And the brown? That's melanoidins, big brown molecules. The inside stays cooler and wetter, so it stays soft and pale. Push it too far, though, and it burns to bitter black char. So what's your perfect toast: pale gold, or nearly burned?
key_facts: The Maillard reaction is between amino acids and reducing sugars and typically proceeds rapidly from around 140 to 165 C (Wikipedia)
Louis Camille Maillard first described it in 1912 (Wikipedia, Chemistry World)
It can produce hundreds of different flavor compounds (Wikipedia, Science ABC)
Melanoidins are the brown molecules; dry heat drives off the bread's water, and excess water slows or halts browning (Science ABC)

package.pinned_comment: If your tongue could smell, what would you follow first?
package.script: A snake's tongue can't taste a thing, so why do you see it flick nonstop? Because it's a scent collector. Each flick grabs tiny particles, from the air and the ground. It pulls back in, and drops them inside the mouth. From there, they reach a special organ, in the roof of the mouth. That's where the smelling happens. Now look at the fork. The two tips spread apart, up to twice as wide as its head. So each tip samples a different spot, like your two ears. If the left tip smells stronger, dinner went left. That's smelling in stereo. In the air, the flicking tongue whips up tiny swirls, that pull smells in, sampling a hundred times more air, than a simple dip. If your tongue could smell, what would you follow first?
key_facts: The tongue has no taste or smell receptors; those are in the vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ in the roof of the mouth (Live Science)

Chemicals are deposited inside the mouth and reach the organ; X-ray work points to floor-of-mouth pads, Schwenk describes tip-to-organ delivery, so the script says only 'inside the mouth' then 'reach'
Tips can spread up to twice the head's width (Live Science)
Each tip compares sides so the brain senses which is stronger (Schwenk, Britannica)
Oscillating flicks create vortices and sample 100 times as much air as a simple downward extension (Live Science)

package.description:

package.pinned_comment: Would you chew your lunch twice, yes or no?
package.script: Cows burp up their lunch on purpose, and you'd never guess why. Grass is really hard to digest. Its walls are made of cellulose, and cows can't break that down alone. So one stomach has four rooms. Room one is the rumen, a vat holding up to forty gallons. It's packed with tiny microbes, and they ferment the grass. Room two, the honeycomb, sorts the pieces. Big chunks go back up her throat, as a soggy ball called cud. She chews it again, for about eight hours a day. Fine mush slides into room three, where water gets squeezed out. Room four is the true stomach, full of acid, like yours. All that fermenting makes gas, hundreds of litres of methane a day, and she burps it out. So, would you chew your lunch twice?
key_facts: One stomach with four compartments: rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum (MSU)
Rumen holds up to 40 gallons in a mature cow (MSU; other sources differ, hence 'up to')
Rumen microbes digest cellulose (MSU, Science Learning Hub)
Reticulum sorts small particles onward, larger stay for further digestion (MSU, Science Learning Hub)
Cows ruminate about a third of the day, ~8 hours (MSU; Purdue 35-40%)
Omasum absorbs water; abomasum is the true stomach with acid (all sources)
Cows burp 250-500 litres of methane a day (Science Learning Hub)

topic.title: How do dolphins sleep without drowning?

package.title: How Do Dolphins Sleep 8 Hours a Day Without Drowning?
package.description:
How do dolphins sleep without drowning when every breath is a choice? They rest one half of the brain at a time with one eye open, and in a 2012 test a dolphin stayed alert for 15 days straight.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-do-whales-and-dolphin/
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/10/121017181244.htm
https://www.mpg.de/10673637/frigatebirds-sleep

package.pinned_comment: If you could keep half your brain awake while the other half slept, what would you use the awake half for?
package.script: You sleep with your whole brain. Dolphins can't: one full nap and they'd drown. So how do they sleep eight hours a day? You pass out at night, and your body keeps breathing without asking. A dolphin doesn't get that deal. Dolphins are mammals, so they breathe air, like you. But every breath is a choice. The blowhole on top of its head is a flap of skin, and scientists think it opens on purpose, not automatically. The dolphin swims up, opens it, breathes out and in, then snaps it shut. So picture one falling fully asleep at sea. Nobody's at the controls. The air stops coming, and the water's right there. So how do you rest a brain that can never switch off? You switch off half of it. It's called unihemispheric sleep, which is a big word for one side at a time. One half of the brain drops into slow, deep waves. The other half stays awake, at low power, running the breathing, and watching for trouble. And you can actually see it from the outside. When the left half sleeps, the right eye closes. When the right half sleeps, the left eye closes. After about two hours, they swap. Each side gets roughly four hours across the day, so a dolphin sleeps about a third of its day, around eight hours. So what does that look like? Two moves. The first is called logging. The dolphin floats at the surface, barely moving, looking exactly like a log. The second is slow swimming, in big circles. In one study of pool dolphins, most of them circled counterclockwise. Breathing slows down too, from around ten breaths a minute, to as few as three. And the open eye has a job. When two dolphins rest side by side, it's the eye that faces the partner. Now, you'd expect half asleep to mean half useless. Researchers tested that in twenty twelve. They had two dolphins spot targets with echolocation, continuously, day and night. Both kept going for five days, with no signs of getting tired. Then the female kept going, for fifteen days. Fifteen, with near-perfect accuracy. Nobody knows how much longer she could've gone, because the test just stopped. So scientists think this trick isn't only about breathing. It may be about staying alert, too. Then there are the newborns. A baby dolphin rests while its mother swims, getting towed along in her slipstream. She can't stop swimming for the first several weeks. One study said mothers and calves barely sleep for a month. Other researchers watched closely, and saw eyes closing during swim rest, so scientists are still arguing about that one. And dolphins aren't alone. Mallard ducks at the edge of a group, keep one eye open, pointed away from the others. Frigatebirds sleep while flying, on trips of up to ten days, averaging just forty-two minutes a day. Back on land, they sleep over twelve hours. So half a brain is a trick nature keeps reusing. One side rests, one side breathes, and nobody drowns. Next question: what actually happens when a jellyfish stings you? It has no brain at all, so who gives the order?
key_facts: Dolphins are conscious breathers; the blowhole flap is thought to open under voluntary control
Unihemispheric sleep: one hemisphere sleeps and the opposite eye closes; sides swap after about two hours
Bottlenose dolphins sleep about 33% of the day by EEG, about four hours per hemisphere
Resting breaths fall from 8-12 to 3-7 a minute
2012 PLOS ONE: two dolphins echolocated for 5 days with no fatigue; the female went 15 days with near-perfect accuracy
Newborn sleep is disputed (Lyamin 2005 vs Sekiguchi and Gnone 2006)
Frigatebirds sleep 42 minutes a day in flight, over 12 hours on land

Why does your foot fall asleep and get pins and needles? It's mostly a squeezed nerve, not cut-off blood flow, and the tingling comes as the nerve starts working again.

package.pinned_comment: Which part of you loses signal first: your foot, your hand, or your arm?
package.script: Why does your foot lose signal when you sit on it? Most people blame blood flow, but scientists call that mostly a myth. The real culprit is a nerve. Think of it like a garden hose, carrying signals instead of water. Messages run from your foot to your brain. So you cross your legs. That pressure pinches the nerve, like stepping on the hose. Signals get blocked, or come through scrambled. Your brain hears almost nothing, so your foot goes numb. Then you stand up. The nerve starts working again, but it isn't smooth yet. Messy signals rush through, and your brain probably reads them as tiny prickles. Those are pins and needles, and they usually fade in minutes. So which part of you loses signal first: your foot, your hand, or your arm?
key_facts: Pressure on a nerve temporarily blocks or disturbs its signals (NTNU's Martin Syvertsen Mykland, Science Norway; UNC's Rebecca Traub, ScienceAlert)
Cut-off blood flow as the cause is called 'mostly a myth' (Science Norway), though sources note blood flow inside the nerve may play a part
The tingling comes as nerves regain function; the exact mechanism isn't fully understood (ScienceAlert, Science Norway)
Pins and needles are usually annoying for a few minutes (Mental Floss)

package.title: How Do Mosquitoes Find You in the Dark From 50 Meters? 🦟
package.description:
How do mosquitoes find you in the dark? They follow the carbon dioxide you breathe out, then your body odor, then the infrared heat from your skin.

package.pinned_comment: Do mosquitoes always pick you, or someone else in your house?
package.script: How does a mosquito find you in the pitch dark? Your breath. Only females hunt you, because they need blood to make eggs. Every time you breathe out, you leave a trail of carbon dioxide. Scientists think she can smell it from up to fifty meters away, about half a football field. She follows that invisible trail. Closer in, she picks up your body odor. In daylight, she'd spot you from about fifteen meters, but tonight, that's no help. So here's her secret weapon. Tiny pits on her antenna tips sense the infrared heat your skin gives off, from about seventy centimeters away. In one lab study, adding that heat doubled how hard mosquitoes searched. Breath, then smell, then heat. And she lands. So tell me: do mosquitoes always pick you, or someone else?

Aedes aegypti detect thermal infrared up to about 70 cm via antenna-tip peg-in-pit structures (Nature 2024).

package.title: How Do Bacteria Turn Milk Into Yogurt in 5 Hours? 🥛
package.description:
How is yogurt made? Two kinds of bacteria eat the lactose in warm milk and make lactic acid, and at about pH 4.6 the milk proteins clump into a soft net that turns thin milk thick.

Sources:
https://ucfoodsafety.ucdavis.edu/sites/g/files/dgvnsk7366/files/inline-files/295482.pdf
https://grupos.eez.csic.es/imili/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/fermented-foods-yoghurt.pdf
https://brodandtaylor.com/the-science-of-great-yogurt/

Animated in the Claymation Set style.

package.pinned_comment: Would you still eat yogurt, knowing bacteria made it?
package.script: Your yogurt is milk that two kinds of bacteria soured in about five hours. First, the milk gets heated, to around two hundred degrees Fahrenheit. That changes its proteins, so they can set together later. Then it cools to about a hundred and ten, and two kinds of bacteria get stirred in. One looks like chains of tiny beads, the other like little rods. They only want one thing: lactose, the sugar in milk. For about five hours, they eat it, and make lactic acid. package.pinned_comment: Have you ever been stung by a jellyfish, and what did it feel like?
package.script: A jellyfish can sting you, in under a millionth of a second, without a brain, and you'd never see it coming. So what actually happens, when one of them stings you? First, meet the animal. Jellyfish have been drifting through the ocean, for more than 500 million years. And they've never had a brain. They also have no heart, no bones, and no blood. What they have instead, is a simple net of nerves, spread through a soft, see-through body. So when a jellyfish stings you, it isn't angry. It isn't even really aware of you. Most of them just drift, and let their tentacles do the work. Now zoom in on one tentacle. It's covered in thousands of tiny stinging cells. And inside each cell sits a capsule, called a nematocyst. Several of them could fit, across a single human hair. Packed inside that capsule, is a long, hollow thread, coiled up like a spring, with a sharp tip waiting at the front. Think of it as a loaded harpoon, sitting in a bath of venom. The pressure in there is huge, about 150 times normal air pressure. That's dozens of times stronger, than the air in a car tire. So what sets it off? Each cell has a tiny trigger on the outside. Bump it, or hit it with the right chemicals, and the lid pops open. Seawater rushes in, the pressure takes over, and the harpoon fires. No brain tells it to. The cell mostly acts on its own. Now here's the part that's hard to believe. In 2006, scientists filmed this, in hydra, a tiny relative of the jellyfish. Their camera shot over a million frames per second. And the first part of the shot, was over in just 700 nanoseconds. That's seven ten-millionths of a second. The tip hit up to five million g's. people tend to black out at around six. And a mantis shrimp's famous punch, reaches about ten thousand. Because that tip is so tiny, the pressure where it lands, is in the range of a bullet. It's strong enough to pierce a crab's shell. So what happens in your skin? After the tip punches in, the thread turns itself inside out, and the capsule squeezes venom through it. Some of those toxins punch holes in cells. Others go after nerves. One cell alone does almost nothing. But brushing a tentacle sets off thousands, all at once, and that's the sudden burn you feel. For most people, it's more painful than dangerous, though a few species, like some box jellyfish, are seriously dangerous. And since nothing here needs a brain, things get strange. A dead jellyfish on the beach, can still sting you. Clownfish live among stinging anemones, the jellyfish's cousins, because their slime lacks a chemical, that helps set those cells off. And some sea slugs eat stinging cells, without firing them, then store them in their own bodies, and use them on their own enemies. So that sting wasn't an attack. It was thousands of tiny machines, each doing the one thing it was built for, half a billion years in the making. Next up, why can you hold a crocodile's jaws shut, with your bare hands?

package.pinned_comment: What's the spiciest chili that's ever fooled you?
package.script:
Chili isn't hot.
You've been fooled every single time.
Put one in the fridge,
and it still burns.
Your tongue is covered in tiny heat alarms.
They stay quiet,
until something hits about forty-three degrees Celsius,
that's a hundred and nine Fahrenheit.
But chili carries a molecule called capsaicin,
and it fits that alarm like a key.
The alarm goes off at body temperature,
and yells to your brain: this is burning!
So you even start to sweat,
but nothing's actually heating up.
Water won't save you,
capsaicin won't mix with it.
Milk's protein, casein, wraps it up,
and carries it away.
Birds don't even feel it,
so they happily eat chilis,
and spread the seeds.
What's the spiciest chili that's ever fooled you?

Birds don't feel capsaicin and spread chili seeds

package.description:
Why do your fingernails keep growing your whole life when your bones stopped growing in your teens? Growth plates in long bones turn to solid bone after puberty, but the nail matrix under your cuticle keeps making new cells, about 3 mm of fingernail a month.

package.pinned_comment: Which grows faster: your fingernails or your toenails?
package.script: Your nails never stop growing, but your arms stopped years ago. So why does one keep going? It starts with your bones. Near each end of a long bone sits a soft strip called a growth plate. It keeps adding new bone, so your arms get longer. But by your late teens, that strip turns to solid bone. The plate closes, and your arms stop for good. Nails work differently. Under your cuticle hides the nail matrix, a tiny factory that never shuts down. It keeps making new cells, pushing the older ones forward. Those cells harden and die, which is why clipping doesn't hurt. Fingernails grow about three millimeters a month, so a whole new nail takes around six months. So which grows faster: your fingernails, or your toenails?

Growth plates ossify and close after puberty, around the late teens
The nail matrix under the cuticle produces new cells throughout life, pushing older ones forward
Nail plate cells harden (keratinize) and are dead, so clipping is painless
Fingernails grow about 3 mm a month; a whole fingernail regrows in about 6 months; toenails grow slower

package.script:
Your stomach acid dissolves metal,
so how does your stomach survive it,
three times a day?
The acid can drop to pH one point five.
Strong enough to eat through zinc,
and turn a steak to mush.
But your stomach has three tricks.
Trick one: a thick blanket of mucus,
loaded with bicarbonate,
basically baking soda.
So right against the wall,
the acid gets neutralized.
Trick two: pepsin, the meat-eating enzyme,
is made switched off.
It only turns on out in the acid,
away from your cells.
Trick three: your lining sheds around half a million cells,
every minute,
and rebuilds itself every few days.
So damage gets replaced before it spreads.
Your stomach isn't acid-proof.
It just heals faster than it melts.
Which trick would you want: the slime, the switch, or the shedding?

A mucus layer rich in bicarbonate neutralizes acid right at the stomach wall
Pepsin is secreted as inactive pepsinogen and is activated by acid in the stomach cavity
The lining sheds roughly 500,000 cells a minute and renews itself every few days (about 3-5 days)

package.title: Why Can Bare Hands Hold Shut a 3,700-Pound Crocodile Bite?
package.description:
A saltwater crocodile has the strongest bite ever measured, about 3,700 pounds of force, yet its jaws can be held shut by hand because the muscles that open them are tiny. We look inside the crocodile jaw, the bite force record, how wildlife handlers use rubber bands and tape, the touch sensors that make croc jaws more sensitive than fingertips, and how alligators replace each tooth up to 50 times.

Sources:
https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/611994
https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2012/11/alligators-and-crocodiles

package.pinned_comment: Which surprised you more: the 3,700-pound bite, or jaws gentle enough to carry babies?
package.script:
Why can your bare hands hold shut
the strongest bite ever measured,
3,700 pounds of crocodile?
It sounds impossible, but it's true.
Let's open up the most lopsided jaw in nature.
Back in 2012, a team of scientists
set out to measure every crocodile on Earth.
All 23 living species,
from tiny caimans to giant gharials.
They wrestled each one
into biting down on a padded force meter.
The winner was the saltwater crocodile.
One big male bit down with about 3,700 pounds of force.
That's more than sixteen thousand newtons.
For comparison, you chew a steak
with maybe 150 to 200 pounds.
Lions, tigers and hyenas
land somewhere around 1,000.
So the saltie bites more than three times harder
than the big cats.
So where does all that power come from?
Look at the back of a crocodile's head.
Those big bulging cheeks aren't fat.
They're almost all jaw-closing muscle,
packed around the hinge
and pulling the lower jaw up like giant rubber bands.
Now look for the muscles that open the jaw.
They're tiny.
A thin little strap
that just tugs the jaw back down.
And that makes sense for how a crocodile eats.
It lies still in the water,
then snaps shut and holds on.
Clamping needs huge force.
Opening only has to lift the jaw's own weight.
So evolution poured almost everything
into closing.
That's the trick behind the bare-hands myth.
Once the jaws are already shut,
the weak opening muscles have to push
against your grip,
and they lose.
Wildlife handlers use this every day.
They loop a strong rubber band around the snout,
or wrap it with a few turns of tape,
and the crocodile simply can't open up.
But please, never try this yourself.
Getting the mouth shut is the dangerous part,
and that tail is all muscle too.
Here's the most surprising part.
Those crushing jaws are also incredibly gentle.
Look closely at a crocodile's face
and you'll see thousands of tiny bumps.
Each bump is a touch sensor,
and scientists found they're more sensitive
than your own fingertips.
They can feel a ripple
from a single drop of water.
They help a crocodile sense prey in the dark,
and they let a mother crocodile
carry her newly hatched babies in her mouth
without hurting a single one.
And then there are the teeth.
An alligator has about 80,
and each one can be replaced up to 50 times
over its long life.
A new tooth is always waiting underneath
the old one.
Scientists are studying how they do it,
hoping it might one day help people
regrow lost teeth.
So the crocodile's jaw is a one-way machine.
Record-breaking power to close,
barely any to open,
and a touch as soft as a fingertip.
Next time, why do porcupine quills
get stuck in you and refuse to come out?

You chew a steak with about 150-200 psi; lions, tigers and hyenas around 1,000 psi (National Geographic)
Croc jaws are mostly jaw-closing muscle; the opening muscles are weak, so hands, rubber bands or tape can hold them shut
Integumentary sensory organs on croc jaws are more sensitive to pressure than human fingertips; used to carry hatchlings (Leitch & Catania 2012)
An alligator can replace each of its ~80 teeth up to 50 times (Smithsonian)

Pandas waste eighty-three percent of the bamboo they eat.

Inside, a panda has a meat-eater's gut,
built just like a bear's:

and no cow-style stomach chambers.

their brain and liver are small,
and they nap a lot.

package.pinned_comment: When a bird dozes on a wire, do you think it's gripping or just balancing?
package.script: A sleeping bird never falls off its branch. You'd never guess why. When a bird bends its legs, tendons behind its ankles pull tight, and that curls the toes around the twig. In songbirds, tiny bumps on those tendons catch on ridges, like a zip tie, so the grip holds with little effort. To let go, it just stands up. But here's the twist. When scientists filmed sleeping starlings, their legs weren't bent enough to lock. They were mostly balancing, probably helped by a balance sensor near their hips, not just their ears. Many birds even sleep with half their brain, one eye open for danger. That's how perching birds, over half of all bird species, nap safely in the trees. So when a bird dozes on a wire, is it gripping, or just balancing?

Many birds sleep with one brain hemisphere at a time and one eye open (ScienceABC, Rattenborg)
Perching birds (passerines) are more than half of all bird species, over 6,000 species (UTK 2019, Encyclopedia.com)

package.script: You've never seen a flamingo eat right-side up. It feeds with its head upside down, because its beak is built backwards. Most birds have a big top beak, and a smaller bottom one. A flamingo's is the other way round. So it flips its head over, and the big lower beak skims the water like a scoop. Inside, the edges are lined with tiny comb-like plates. Then the tongue starts pumping, about four or five times a second, like a little piston. Water squirts out through the combs, and tiny shrimp and algae get trapped inside. Flamingos even stomp in the mud, to stir up little whirlpools full of food. And those shrimp and algae? They're packed with pink pigments. That's what turns a flamingo pink. So, would you eat upside down, if it turned you pink?

tags: why do baby teeth fall out
package.pinned_comment: Which baby tooth did you lose first: a front one on the bottom, like most kids, or something else?
package.script:
Every baby tooth you ever lost,
was secretly eaten.
By what?
Kids have twenty baby teeth.
Adults have thirty-two.
But a tiny jaw can't fit big adult teeth,
so the new ones wait,
hidden in the bone underneath.
Around age six,
an adult tooth starts pushing up.
That pressure wakes up special cells,
called odontoclasts.
They dissolve the baby tooth's root,
bit by bit.
No root means nothing holding on,
so it wobbles,
and pops out.
That's why a lost baby tooth,
looks like it has no root at all.
It got eaten.
Then the adult tooth slides into the gap.
By about age twelve,
most baby teeth are gone.
So which of yours got eaten first?

Permanent teeth develop in the jawbone beneath the baby teeth
Pressure from the erupting adult tooth activates odontoclasts that resorb the baby tooth's root
With its root resorbed, the baby tooth loosens and falls out, usually starting around age 6
Most baby teeth are lost by about age 12

topic.title: Why do your knuckles crack?

package.title: Why Do Your Knuckles Crack? 🫧
package.description:
Why do knuckles crack? Pulling a finger joint apart drops the pressure in its fluid, so dissolved gas forms a bubble with a pop, and it takes about 20 minutes before that knuckle can crack again.

Sources:

https://www.snexplores.org/article/mystery-solved-why-knuckles-crack

package.pinned_comment: How many times have you cracked your knuckles today? Be honest 👀
package.script:
Your knuckle crack is actually a gas bubble,
and it can't happen again for twenty minutes.
Every finger joint sits in a tiny capsule,
filled with a slippery fluid.
That fluid has gas dissolved in it,
like a soda with the cap on.
When you pull or bend the joint,
the capsule stretches,
and the pressure inside drops.
The gas rushes out of the fluid,
and a bubble forms, with a pop!
In 2015, scientists filmed it in an MRI scanner,
and saw the bubble appear right at the crack.
Try that knuckle again, and... nothing.
The bubble needs about twenty minutes
to dissolve back into the fluid.
And no, studies say it won't give you arthritis.
One doctor cracked only his left hand's knuckles
for sixty years,
and both hands stayed the same.
So, how many bubbles have you made today?

It takes about 20 minutes before the same knuckle can crack again
Dr. Donald Unger cracked only his left hand's knuckles for about 60 years and found no arthritis in either hand (2009 Ig Nobel)

package.title: Why Your Taste Buds Die Every 10 Days
package.description:
How do taste buds work, why is the tongue map a myth, and why do your taste cells get replaced about every 10 days? A simple explainer of papillae, taste receptors, the five basic tastes (sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami), why smell makes most of flavor, and the catfish with 175,000 taste buds.

Sources:
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/24684-taste-buds
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue_map
https://www.livescience.com/32970-what-animal-has-the-best-sense-of-taste.html

package.pinned_comment: Were you taught the tongue map in school? Tell me which flavor you were told lives on the tip!
package.script: Your taste buds die every ten days, and nobody ever told you why. Right now, thousands of tiny sensors are tasting your own spit. So what are they, how do they work, and what about that tongue map from school? Let's start with the map. You've probably seen it. Sweet on the tip, bitter at the back, sour and salty on the sides. It's a myth. In nineteen oh one, a German scientist named David Hanig found that some spots were just a tiny bit more sensitive. Then in nineteen forty two, his graph got redrawn, and people read it the wrong way. The truth? Every part of your tongue that has taste buds can taste all five flavors. So where are the taste buds? Stick out your tongue in a mirror. Those little bumps are not taste buds. They're called papillae, and most taste buds hide inside them, along the sides of each bump. An adult has somewhere between two thousand and ten thousand taste buds. A few even live on the roof of your mouth and down in your throat. Now zoom in on one bud. It looks a bit like a tiny onion, packed with fifty to one hundred fifty taste cells. At the top there's a little opening, called a taste pore. When you eat, food dissolves in your spit, and those molecules slip into the pore. Each taste cell has receptors on its tip, like locks waiting for the right key. Sugar fits the sweet lock. Salt slips through its own little channel. When a key fits, the cell fires a signal down a nerve, and your brain says, sweet! And here's the clever part. Each of the five tastes has a job. Sweet means energy. Salty means minerals your body needs. Sour can mean unripe, or spoiled. Bitter is a warning, because lots of poisons taste bitter. And umami means protein. That fifth taste was found in nineteen oh eight, by a Japanese chemist named Kikunae Ikeda. He wondered why seaweed soup tasted so rich, and found the answer was glutamate. But taste is only half the story. Hold your nose and eat a jelly bean. You can tell it's sweet, but not what flavor it is. That's because most of what we call flavor actually comes from smell. And some animals put us to shame. A catfish can have up to one hundred seventy five thousand taste buds, all over its body. It's basically a swimming tongue. Now, back to that hook. Your taste cells work in a wet, rough place, getting scraped by crunchy food, and burned by hot soup. So your body replaces them, about every ten days. That's why a burned tongue feels normal again so fast. Every bite you take, thousands of brand new taste cells are on the job. Next time, why do some people get carsick, while others feel totally fine?

package.pinned_comment: Could you sleep standing up, or would you fall flat on your face?
package.script: A 500-kilo horse can sleep standing up, and you'd never guess why it doesn't fall. The trick is called the stay apparatus. Tendons and ligaments brace its legs, so the joints lock with almost no muscle effort. In a back leg, the kneecap hooks over a bump on the thigh bone, like a latch clicking shut. The other back leg gets to rest, and every so often it swaps sides. But there's a catch. Dreaming sleep, called REM, relaxes every muscle, and that unlocks the legs. So for REM, a horse has to lie down, about thirty to forty-five minutes a day, often while a buddy stands guard. Miss it for a week or so, and its knees can buckle mid-nap. So, could you sleep standing up, or would you fall flat on your face?

In the hind leg the kneecap (patella) hooks over the medial ridge of the femur to lock the stifle; the horse rests the other hind leg and swaps (standard equine anatomy; TheHorse on the stay apparatus)
REM sleep relaxes all muscle tone, including the stay apparatus, so horses must lie down (sternal or lateral) for it (TheHorse, SmartPak)
Horses need about 30 (SmartPak) to 40-45 (TheHorse) minutes of REM per day; script says 'about thirty to forty-five minutes'
In wild herds one horse often stays awake on watch while others lie down (TheHorse, SmartPak); script hedges with 'often'
REM deprivation lasting more than a week or so can make horses drift into REM standing and collapse, with bowing knees (Houpt and Greening via TheHorse)
Average horse weight ~500 kg (common figure for a riding horse)

A tick glues itself into your skin in thirty minutes,

package.title: Why Do 1 in 3 People Get Carsick? 🚗
package.description:
Why do some people get carsick while others can read in the back seat? Motion sickness explained in simple words: how your eyes and inner ear (the vestibular system) disagree, the poison theory, the genes behind it, and why the driver almost never feels sick.

Sources:

package.pinned_comment: Do you get carsick, or are you the one reading a book in the back seat? 🚗
package.script: Every time you get carsick, your brain thinks you've swallowed poison. And for one in three people, that alarm goes off on almost every ride. So why does the back seat wreck some of us, while others read a whole book and feel totally fine? To find out, we need to look inside your head. You know how you're moving using two main systems. Your eyes are one. The other is hidden deep inside each ear. It's called the vestibular system, and it's basically a built-in motion sensor. Three tiny loops filled with fluid sense every time your head turns. And two little sacs lined with tiny crystals feel you speed up, slow down and tip. Most of the time your eyes and ears agree. But picture yourself in the back seat, reading a phone. Your eyes see a screen that isn't moving. Your inner ear feels every bump and every curve. One says still. The other says moving. Scientists call this sensory conflict, and it's the leading explanation for motion sickness. So why would a mixed-up signal make you feel sick? One popular theory goes way back to our ancestors. Long ago, if your senses suddenly stopped agreeing, a likely cause was something toxic you'd eaten. So the brain may have learned a simple rule. Signals don't match? Empty the stomach. Researchers still debate this idea, but it would explain why a bumpy ride can feel a lot like food poisoning. Here's where it gets personal. In 2015 the genetics company 23andMe studied more than eighty thousand people. They found thirty-five spots in our DNA linked to motion sickness. And some studies suggest up to seventy percent of the difference between people comes down to genes. Age matters too. Kids between about seven and twelve get it the most, and lots of people grow out of the worst of it. Women report it more often than men, and so do people who get migraines. So if your whole family turns green on road trips, that's probably not a coincidence. Now for the strangest part. People who have completely lost the motion sensors in their inner ears basically don't get motion sick at all. No inner ear signal, no conflict, no alarm. What you can see matters too. One study found that passengers who couldn't see the road ahead were about three times more likely to feel sick. And the driver? Usually fine. The driver knows every turn before it happens, so the brain isn't caught by surprise. This old alarm is now facing brand new problems. Virtual reality flips the conflict around. Your eyes see motion, but your body sits perfectly still. And as cars start driving themselves, everyone becomes a passenger, staring at screens instead of the road. So engineers are testing tricks, like lights that hint at the next turn, to help your eyes and ears agree again. So the next time a car ride makes you queasy, remember, your brain isn't broken. It's just protecting you from a poison that isn't there. Next time, what really happens if a porcupine's quills get stuck in you?

Heritability estimates for motion sickness range up to about 70%
Children about 7-12 are most susceptible; it is more common in women and in people with migraines
People with complete loss of vestibular function are essentially immune to motion sickness
Passengers without a view of the road ahead were about 3 times more likely to get sick

topic.title: Why does garlic breath last a whole day?

package.title: Why Does Garlic Breath Last 24 Hours? 🧄
package.description:
Why does garlic breath last so long? One garlic gas, allyl methyl sulfide, isn't broken down by your gut or liver, so it travels in your blood and comes out through your lungs and sweat for up to a day, which is why mouthwash can't fix it.

package.script:
Your garlic breath can leak out of your lungs for twenty-four hours. Why?
Mouthwash won't stop it.
Crush a clove of garlic
and it lets off a bunch of stinky sulfur gases.
Most break down fast.
But one is sneaky.
It's called allyl methyl sulfide.
Your gut and liver barely touch it,
so it slips into your blood
and rides around your whole body.
Each time that blood passes through your lungs,
a little leaks out on your breath.
Some even sneaks out through your sweat.
Three hours after dinner,
it's the main garlic smell you're breathing out.
And it keeps that up for hours and hours.
Raw apple, mint or milk can help a little.
So really,
garlic breath is garlic blood.

topic.title: How do owls fly without making a sound?

package.title: Why You Can't Hear an Owl Until It's 3 Feet Away 🦉
package.description:
How do owls fly without making a sound? Comb-like serrations on the wing's leading edge, a soft trailing-edge fringe and velvety feathers break up and hush the air swirls that make most birds' wings whoosh, so a barn owl's flight stays quiet in the range a mouse can hear.

Sources:

https://knowablemagazine.org/article/technology/2020/how-owls-fly-without-making-a-sound

package.script: Why can't you hear an owl until it's three feet from you? Most birds' wings churn the air into big swirls, and those swirls are the whoosh you hear. But an owl's front wing feathers have a comb, tiny teeth along the edge. They split the air into small, quiet streams. Then a soft, ragged fringe on the back edge and a velvety coat on top hush whatever noise is left. Big wings help too. A barn owl can fly as slowly as two miles an hour, and slower means quieter. Its wings mute the high sounds above sixteen hundred hertz, right where a mouse's hearing begins. So the mouse never hears it coming, but the owl hears the mouse just fine. If an owl flew over you tonight, do you think you'd hear it?

A soft trailing-edge fringe and a velvety feather texture further dampen the noise (Audubon; Knowable/Smithsonian)
A barn owl's swoosh is below the threshold of human hearing until the owl is about three feet away (Knowable/Smithsonian)
Large wings relative to body mass let owls fly as slowly as about 2 mph for a barn owl (Audubon)
Owl wings mute frequencies above about 1,600 Hz, roughly where rodent hearing begins (Knowable/Smithsonian)

topic.title: Why do geese fly in a V?

package.title: Why Do Geese Fly in a V? 🪿
package.description:
Why do geese fly in a V? Each bird rides the rising air that curls off the wingtip of the bird ahead, which saves energy: pelicans flying in formation had heart rates up to 14% lower, and ibises take turns in the tiring front spot.

Sources:
https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/birds-that-fly-in-a-v-formation-use-an-amazing-trick
https://www.ox.ac.uk/node/29050
https://www.audubon.org/magazine/why-birds-fly-v-formation-migration-science

tags: why do geese fly in a v
package.pinned_comment: Would you rather be the leader at the front of the V, or the bird riding in the back?
package.script:
Birds in a V can cut their heart rate 14 percent,
and you've never seen why.
It's the secret behind every V of geese.
Each flap pushes air down behind the wing.
But at the wingtip, air curls up and around,
into a spinning swirl.
Just outside that swirl, the air is rising.
So the bird behind slides into that exact spot,
and gets free lift on every flap.
Line everyone up like that,
and you get a V.
Pelicans tracked in formation
had heart rates up to 14 percent lower than flying solo.
Ibises even time their flaps to match the bird ahead.
But the front bird gets no free ride.
So ibises take turns,
swapping the tiring spot at the front.
Honestly, that's teamwork with zero meetings.
So which bird would you rather be,
the leader at the front, or the one in the back?

Northern bald ibises time their wingbeats to match the upwash of the bird ahead (Portugal et al. 2014)

package.script: Why does your dog tilt its head? Genius dogs do it twenty times more. In Budapest, scientists tested some genius border collies that know the names of over ten toys. When their owner said a toy's name, those genius dogs tilted their heads forty-three percent of the time. Regular dogs? Just two percent. So the tilt might be a dog matching your word to a picture in its head. But there's another idea. A dog's snout blocks part of your face, especially your mouth. Tilting gives it a clearer view. In one survey, seventy-one percent of long-snouted dogs often tilted, but only fifty-two percent of flat-faced dogs did. And here's the fun part: each dog usually tilts to the same side, every time. So which way does your dog tilt, left or right?

package.script:
A porcupine carries 30,000 tiny harpoons.
So what happens when one sticks into you?
And why won't it come back out?
Let's take a really close look at the pointiest coat in nature.
First, let's bust the biggest myth.
Porcupines can't shoot their quills.
Not even a little.
People have believed it since ancient Greece,
but it just isn't true.
A North American porcupine wears about 30,000 quills
on its back, sides and tail.
Each one is a stiff, hollow hair,
made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
They're up to four inches long,
and they're only loosely attached to the skin.
So the porcupine doesn't throw anything.
An attacker bumps into it,
the quills grab hold,
and they pull straight out of the porcupine.
Now let's zoom in on the very tip of one quill.
Under a microscope, it's covered in hundreds of tiny barbs,
all pointing backwards, like the scales on a pine cone.
In 2012, scientists pushed quills into meat in the lab.
The barbs did something surprising.
They cut the force needed to go in by about half.
The tiny barbs grip the tissue and slice it,
a bit like the teeth on a bread knife.
So the quill slides in deep and easy.
Then they tried pulling them out.
Now the barbs flare open and snag,
and it took about four times more force
than a smooth quill.
In, easy. Out, really hard.
Just like a fishhook.
Less than half a centimeter in,
and it's already holding on.
And here's the sneaky part.
A quill that's stuck doesn't just sit there.
Every time the animal moves,
its own muscles squeeze around the barbs,
and each one can only ratchet one way.
Forward.
So a stuck quill slowly works its way deeper.
That's why a dog that noses a porcupine
needs a trip to the vet, and fast.
But here's the thing.
A porcupine would much rather not fight at all.
It gives you plenty of warning first.
It growls.
It chatters its teeth.
It raises its black and white quills
like a giant pincushion.
And it releases a smell from a patch on its lower back.
One scientist said it smells a bit like goat,
or a strange, stinky cheese.
If you still don't back off,
it turns around and swings its tail.
Thwack.
And there's one more twist.
Porcupines sometimes stab themselves,
like when they fall out of a tree.
So their quills come coated in greasy fats
that fight off germs.
Built-in antibiotic.
Scientists love these quills.
The same team that tested the barbs
is copying them for medical needles and staples
that slide in gently
and hold on tight.
So a porcupine's quill is a hair
that works like a fishhook,
goes in easy, comes out hard,
and keeps itself clean.
Not bad for a hair.
Next time, how does a homing pigeon
find its way home from hundreds of miles away?

package.title: Why Do Zebras Have Stripes? 🦓
package.description:
Why do zebras have stripes? Scientists filmed biting horseflies around zebras and horses and found the flies landed on zebras less than a quarter as often, because the stripes seem to stop them braking for a landing.

Sources:

package.script:
Zebra stripes stop 3 out of 4 fly landings,
and you can see why.
In Africa, biting horseflies swarm grazing animals,
and their bites can spread nasty diseases.
So researchers in Britain filmed flies
buzzing around zebras and horses.
The flies flew up to both just as often.
But they landed on zebras less than a quarter as often.
So what's going on?
Near a horse, a fly slows down for a soft landing.
Near a zebra, the stripes seem to scramble its eyes,
so it never brakes,
and it bumps right off or zooms past.
Then they dressed horses in striped coats.
Flies kept missing the coats,
but still landed on their bare heads.
Honestly, that's kind of genius.
Camouflage? Keeping cool? The evidence for those is weaker.
So would you wear stripes to your next picnic?

package.description:

Not water: a dromedary's hump stores up to about 35 kg of fat for energy, while its water is spread through its whole body, it can lose about a quarter of its weight in water, and then drink around 100 litres in roughly ten minutes thanks to oval red blood cells that can swell without bursting.

package.description:
What is the crusty 'sleep' in your eyes every morning? Eye crust, or rheum, is mucus, oil, dust and dead skin cells that your blinks normally wash away, but when you sleep the blinking stops, so it collects in the corners of your eyes and dries out.

package.script:
You wake up with dead skin glued in your eyes.
Why?
All day, your eyes wear a thin film of tears,
made of water, sticky mucus and a little oil.
Dust and old skin cells get trapped in it.
But you blink about 15 to 20 times a minute.
That's over 14,000 blinks a day,
and every blink washes that gunk away.
Then you fall asleep,
and the blinking stops.
Now the mucus, oil, dust and dead skin have nowhere to go.
They drift into the corners of your eyes,
and overnight they dry out
into crusty little flakes.
Doctors call it rheum.
And a little every morning is totally normal.
Honestly, it's just yesterday's cleanup, waiting for you.
So what do you call it: sleep, eye boogers, or crust?

The tear film is made of water, mucus and oil
A little morning crust is normal (Cleveland Clinic)
